group.passage:
Humpback whales have their own method of cultural evolution that spans long distances, according to a recent study conducted by Ellen Garland and her teams in Ecuador. The study indicated that whale songs [[1]] heard off the eastern coast of Australia were recorded again in Ecuador several years later. Tracking the movements of these melodies, researchers discovered that whales in Australia could pass their songs to others in French Polynesia, which [[2]] gave songs to those in Ecuador. This shows that Humpback whales are able to transmit songs among different groups across the South Pacific Ocean.
It is believed that the whale songs spread when neighboring groups of whales [[3]] of each other’s acoustic signals during their migrations between breeding and feeding grounds. Suggesting the whale songs may be part of a “cultural network” in the South Pacific Ocean, the research team leader Ellen Garland refers to the transmission of whale songs from Australia to Ecuador as a remarkable [[4]] of the cultural network puzzle in the southern hemisphere.
The researchers aim to collaborate with other research groups to investigate whale song transmission beyond the South Pacific basin. By linking different ocean basins together, they hope to explore whether similar dynamics are [[5]] outside this region. This deeper understanding of whale song transmission could contribute to our knowledge of communication evolution, including the development of complex human speech.

tags.topic: cultural transmission of humpback whale songs across the South Pacific
